question.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=1$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{1-\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{1-{1}^{2}}{1-\sqrt{1}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{1-\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}\frac{(1-{x}^{2})(1+\sqrt{x})}{(1-\sqrt{x})(1+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}\frac{(1-x)(1+x)(1+\sqrt{x})}{({1}^{2}-{(\sqrt{x})}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}\frac{(1-x)(1+x)(1+\sqrt{x})}{(1-x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(1+x)(1+\sqrt{x}) \\  & =(1+1)(1+\sqrt{1}) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
